Why Do Dentures Become Loose Over Time?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

If you wear dentures, you may have noticed that what once felt like a secure, comfortable fit has gradually started to feel less stable. Loose dentures are one of the most common concerns raised by denture wearers, and it is entirely understandable why so many people turn to online searches for reassurance and answers.

Understanding why dentures become loose over time is an important step towards maintaining your oral comfort and overall wellbeing. In most cases, the loosening is not the result of a fault with the dentures themselves but rather a natural process that occurs within the mouth after teeth are lost. Changes to the jawbone, gum tissues, and the denture materials themselves can all contribute to a gradual decline in fit.

This article explains the main reasons why dentures may lose their stability, what happens inside the mouth over the months and years following tooth loss, and when it may be appropriate to seek a professional dental assessment. Whether you are a long-term denture wearer or have recently begun wearing dentures, the information below may help you better understand your oral health and the options available to you.

Dentures become loose over time primarily because of a natural process called bone resorption. After teeth are removed, the jawbone no longer receives the stimulation it needs to maintain its density and volume. Over months and years, the bone gradually shrinks, causing the gum ridge that supports the denture to change shape. As the underlying bone and soft tissue alter, the denture no longer conforms to the mouth as precisely as it once did, resulting in movement, discomfort, and reduced stability.

The Role of Bone Resorption in Denture Loosening

One of the primary reasons dentures become loose is a biological process known as alveolar bone resorption. When natural teeth are present, the roots transmit biting and chewing forces into the jawbone. This mechanical stimulation signals the body to continually renew and maintain bone density in the jaw. Once teeth are extracted, however, that stimulation is lost.

Without the functional loading provided by tooth roots, the body begins to gradually reabsorb the alveolar bone â€” the ridge of bone that previously supported the teeth and now supports the denture. Research suggests that the most significant bone loss typically occurs within the first year following extraction, although the process continues at a slower rate over subsequent years.

This ongoing reduction in bone volume means the shape of the jaw ridge changes over time. Because dentures are crafted to fit the mouth at a specific point in time, even small changes in bone contour can lead to noticeable looseness. The lower jaw tends to experience more pronounced resorption than the upper jaw, which is one reason why lower dentures are often reported as less stable than upper ones.

How Gum Tissue Changes Affect Denture Fit

In addition to changes in the underlying bone, the soft tissues of the mouth also undergo alterations that can influence how well dentures fit. The gum tissue that sits over the jaw ridge may become thinner, less resilient, or change in shape as the years pass. General health, nutrition, medication use, and ageing can all play a role in the condition of oral soft tissues.

Certain medications, for example, may cause dry mouth, which reduces the thin film of saliva that normally helps create a gentle suction between the denture and the gum. This loss of moisture can make dentures feel less secure. Similarly, conditions that affect the body's connective tissues or immune response may influence the health of the gums and the mucous membranes that line the mouth.

Weight fluctuations can also affect the soft tissue in the mouth. Significant weight loss, in particular, may reduce the volume of tissue supporting the denture, contributing to a looser fit. These changes are typically gradual, which means many patients do not notice the difference immediately but become aware of it over a period of weeks or months.

Signs That Your Dentures May Need Attention

Recognising the early signs of an ill-fitting denture can help you seek advice before more significant problems develop. Some common indicators that your dentures may no longer fit as well as they should include:

  • Increased movement when eating, speaking, or yawning
  • Sore spots or irritation on the gums, particularly in areas where the denture presses unevenly
  • Difficulty chewing certain foods that you could previously manage comfortably
  • A clicking sound when you talk or eat, caused by the denture lifting away from the gum
  • The need for increasing amounts of denture adhesive to achieve a stable fit
  • Changes in your bite or the way your upper and lower dentures meet

If you experience any of these signs, it does not necessarily indicate a serious problem, but it is worth having your dentures and oral health reviewed by a dental professional. Early assessment can often lead to straightforward adjustments that restore comfort.

The Science Behind Jawbone Changes After Tooth Loss

To understand why the jawbone changes, it helps to know a little about how bone behaves in the body. Bone is living tissue that constantly remodels itself through a balance of two processes: bone formation (carried out by cells called osteoblasts) and bone resorption (carried out by cells called osteoclasts). In a healthy mouth with natural teeth, the forces of chewing stimulate the osteoblasts to maintain bone density.

When teeth are lost and replaced with conventional dentures, the denture sits on top of the gum rather than within the bone. The forces transmitted through the denture are distributed across the surface of the gum ridge rather than being directed into the bone through tooth roots. This fundamentally different loading pattern means the osteoblast activity decreases, while osteoclast activity continues, leading to a net loss of bone over time.

The rate of bone loss varies from person to person and can be influenced by factors including age, overall health, nutritional status, and whether the patient wears their dentures continuously (including overnight). Some studies suggest that wearing dentures around the clock may accelerate bone loss compared to removing them at night, as the constant pressure on the gum ridge does not allow the tissues adequate time to recover.

Denture Wear and Material Changes

It is not only the mouth that changes over time â€” the dentures themselves undergo wear. The acrylic resin used to create denture bases can gradually warp, become slightly porous, or develop microscopic surface changes that affect the fit and hygiene of the appliance. The artificial teeth on the denture also wear down with use, which can alter the way the upper and lower dentures meet and distribute biting forces.

These material changes, combined with the biological changes occurring in the mouth, can compound the problem of looseness. A denture that has warped even slightly will not conform accurately to the gum ridge, and worn teeth may change the balance of the bite, placing uneven pressure on certain areas of the ridge and potentially accelerating localised bone loss.

Regular dental reviews allow your dentist to assess both the condition of your dentures and the health of your oral tissues, helping to identify when a reline, adjustment, or replacement may be beneficial.

Options for Improving Denture Stability

If your dentures have become loose, there are several approaches that a dental professional may consider following a clinical assessment. The most appropriate option will depend on the extent of the changes in your mouth and the current condition of your dentures.

Denture relining is a common procedure in which the fitting surface of the denture is reshaped with new material to match the current contour of your gum ridge. This can significantly improve the fit without requiring entirely new dentures.

Denture rebasing involves replacing the entire base of the denture whilst retaining the existing teeth. This may be recommended when the base material has deteriorated beyond the point where a simple reline would be effective.

New dentures may be recommended if the existing set has worn significantly or if the changes in the mouth are too substantial for relining to address.

For patients experiencing persistent difficulties with denture stability, dental implants may be discussed as a potential option. Implants are small titanium posts placed into the jawbone that can support dentures, crowns, or bridges. Because they integrate with the bone, they also help to maintain bone density in the jaw. However, suitability for implant treatment depends entirely on individual clinical assessment.

When Professional Dental Assessment May Be Needed

There are certain situations where seeking a dental evaluation is particularly advisable. Consider arranging an appointment if you notice:

  • Persistent soreness or ulceration of the gums that does not resolve within a few days
  • A noticeable change in the way your dentures fit, particularly if the change occurs suddenly
  • Difficulty speaking clearly due to denture movement
  • Discomfort or pain in the jaw joint
  • Any unusual lumps, patches, or changes in the soft tissues of your mouth

These symptoms do not necessarily indicate a serious condition, but a dental professional can provide a thorough examination to assess your oral health and the fit of your dentures. Early attention to changes in fit can help prevent secondary issues such as gum irritation, difficulty eating, and nutritional concerns that may arise from avoiding certain foods.

It is generally recommended that denture wearers attend regular dental check-ups, even if they have no remaining natural teeth. Your dentist will examine the soft tissues, assess the fit of your dentures, and check for any changes that may require attention. If you are considering whether implant-retained dentures might be suitable for your situation, a clinical consultation can help determine whether this is an appropriate option for you.

Prevention and Oral Health Advice for Denture Wearers

Whilst some degree of bone resorption is a natural consequence of tooth loss, there are steps you can take to help maintain your oral health and potentially extend the comfortable life of your dentures.

  • Remove your dentures at night to give your gum tissues time to rest and recover from the pressure of wearing dentures during the day.
  • Clean your dentures daily using a soft brush and appropriate denture cleaning solution. Avoid using abrasive toothpaste, which can scratch the surface and harbour bacteria.
  • Clean your gums and any remaining teeth thoroughly each day. A soft-bristled toothbrush or damp cloth can be used to gently clean the gum ridges, tongue, and palate.
  • Attend regular dental appointments, even if you wear full dentures. Your dentist can monitor changes in your oral tissues and the fit of your dentures.
  • Maintain a balanced diet that supports bone and tissue health. Adequate calcium, vitamin D, and overall nutrition play a role in maintaining bone density.
  • Avoid using excessive denture adhesive as a long-term solution for loose dentures. If you find you need increasing amounts of adhesive, this may indicate that a professional assessment is needed.
  • Handle your dentures carefully to avoid dropping or warping them. When not in use, store them in water or a denture soaking solution.

Key Points to Remember

  • Dentures commonly become loose over time due to natural changes in the jawbone and gum tissues following tooth loss.
  • Bone resorption is the primary biological cause, as the jaw gradually loses volume without the stimulation of natural tooth roots.
  • Gum tissue changes, denture material wear, and general health factors also contribute to a declining fit.
  • Regular dental reviews are important for all denture wearers, even those without natural teeth remaining.
  • Several options exist to improve denture stability, including relining, rebasing, new dentures, or implant-supported solutions, depending on individual suitability.
  • Good denture care and oral hygiene can help maintain comfort and support overall oral health.

Frequently Asked Questions

How often should dentures be replaced?

As a general guideline, dentures may need to be replaced approximately every five to ten years, although this varies depending on individual circumstances. The rate of bone resorption, the condition of the denture materials, and changes in your oral health all influence how long a set of dentures will remain effective. Regular dental check-ups allow your dentist to assess whether your dentures are still providing a satisfactory fit and function. In some cases, a reline or adjustment may extend the useful life of existing dentures without the need for a full replacement.

Can denture adhesive fix loose dentures permanently?

Denture adhesive can provide temporary improvement in stability and may be helpful in certain situations, but it is not intended as a permanent solution for dentures that no longer fit properly. If you find yourself relying on increasing amounts of adhesive to keep your dentures in place, this is often a sign that the fit has changed significantly and a dental assessment may be beneficial. A dental professional can evaluate the cause of the looseness and recommend appropriate options, which may include relining, adjusting, or replacing the dentures.

Is bone loss in the jaw preventable after tooth loss?

Some degree of bone resorption is considered a natural consequence of tooth loss and cannot be entirely prevented with conventional dentures. However, the rate of bone loss may be influenced by factors such as general health, nutrition, and denture-wearing habits. Dental implants, where clinically suitable, can help preserve bone density because they integrate with the jawbone and provide stimulation similar to natural tooth roots. Whether implants are appropriate depends on individual assessment, including the amount of available bone and overall health status.

Why does my lower denture feel less stable than the upper one?

Lower dentures are frequently reported as less stable than upper dentures. This is partly because the upper denture covers a larger surface area, including the palate, which creates a broader base for suction and retention. The lower jaw ridge is typically narrower and is subject to greater forces from the tongue and cheek muscles. Additionally, the lower jaw often experiences more significant bone resorption than the upper jaw. These anatomical factors combine to make achieving a stable fit for lower dentures more challenging, and this is one of the most common reasons patients explore implant-retained options.

Should I wear my dentures while sleeping?

Most dental professionals recommend removing your dentures at night. Wearing dentures continuously can place sustained pressure on the gum tissues and underlying bone, which may contribute to faster bone resorption and increase the risk of fungal infections such as oral thrush. Removing dentures at night allows the tissues to rest, recover, and benefit from the natural cleansing action of saliva. Clean your dentures before storing them in water or a recommended soaking solution overnight, and clean your gums and oral tissues before going to bed.

Can loose dentures cause other health problems?

Loose dentures can contribute to several secondary concerns. Poorly fitting dentures may cause sore spots, ulceration, and chronic irritation of the gum tissues. They can also make eating certain foods difficult, which may lead some patients to limit their diet to softer foods and potentially miss out on important nutrients. Difficulty speaking clearly can affect confidence and social interactions. In some cases, chronic irritation from ill-fitting dentures may contribute to changes in the oral tissues that warrant professional evaluation. Maintaining a good denture fit through regular dental reviews can help reduce these risks.

Conclusion

Loose dentures are a common experience for many people who wear them, and understanding why this happens can help you take proactive steps to maintain your oral comfort and health. The natural process of bone resorption following tooth loss is the primary reason dentures become loose over time, but changes in gum tissue, denture material wear, and general health factors all play a contributing role.

Regular dental check-ups remain one of the most valuable steps you can take as a denture wearer. A dental professional can monitor the changes occurring in your mouth, assess the condition of your dentures, and discuss options that may help improve fit and function when needed.

If you have noticed that your dentures feel less secure than they once did, or if you are experiencing discomfort, it is worth seeking professional advice. Early assessment can often lead to straightforward solutions that restore comfort and confidence.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

This article is intended for general educational purposes and does not constitute dental advice. Individual circumstances vary, and treatment suitability can only be determined through a professional clinical assessment.
